00 What is cache CONCEPT
A cache is a fast storage layer that holds the results of expensive computations or queries so that subsequent requests get a response without repeating the work. The rule is simple: if retrieving a result again is cheaper than computing it from scratch — cache it. Caching exists at every level of a modern system, from the CPU to the browser.
ANALOGY

Think of a restaurant. The chef takes 20 minutes to prepare a complex dish. If orders keep coming in for the same dish, it makes sense to keep a ready portion in a warming cabinet (cache) rather than cook it from scratch every time. Cache hit — the dish is in the cabinet. Cache miss — the cabinet is empty, cooking must start.

What is cached where

LayerWhat is cached
BrowserHTML, JS, CSS, images, Cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage
CDNStatic assets, HTML pages (when appropriate headers are set)
Reverse Proxy (Nginx)HTTP responses from backend services, static files
ApplicationBusiness logic results, aggregated data (in-memory or Redis)
DatabaseQuery results (query cache), page buffers (InnoDB buffer pool)
CPUInstructions and data (L1 / L2 / L3 cache — outside QA scope)

Cache hit and cache miss

CACHE HIT
The requested data is already in the cache and has not expired (TTL has not elapsed). The response is returned immediately from the cache without touching the source. Fast, cheap — this is the whole point of caching.
CACHE MISS
The data is absent from the cache or has gone stale. The system fetches it from the original source (database, API), returns the response, and usually stores it in the cache for next time.

TTL — Time To Live

TTL (Time To Live) is the duration for which cached data is considered fresh. Once TTL expires the data is treated as stale and the next request will result in a cache miss. TTL can range from seconds to hours depending on how critical data freshness is for that particular resource.

WHY THIS MATTERS FOR QA

Cache is the most common cause of "weird behavior" that is hard to reproduce. A test passes in one run and fails in the next. A feature "doesn't work" — in reality the browser or CDN is serving an old version. Always check the cache before filing a bug.

01 Cache in the request path — 7 layers COMPONENT
↑ top
Every request from the client to the database passes through several layers, each of which may have its own cache. Understanding these layers helps a QA engineer precisely identify where a response came from — and whether it is current. 
Client request
      ↓
[1] Client-side state  (cookie, localStorage, sessionStorage, Redux/Zustand)
      ↓ miss
[2] HTTP Browser Cache  (Cache-Control, ETag, 304 Not Modified)
      ↓ miss
[3] CDN / Proxy Cache  (Cloudflare, Fastly, Nginx)
      ↓ miss
[4] API Gateway Cache
      ↓ miss
[5] App In-memory Cache  (LRU Map, Caffeine, node-lru-cache)
      ↓ miss
[6] Redis / Distributed Cache
      ↓ miss
[7] Database
      ↓
Response → stored in cache ↑ for the next request

Layer 1 — Client-side state

Data stored directly in the browser or client application: cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, Redux/Zustand/Pinia state. Used to avoid making an HTTP request at all — the data is already on the client.

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 1
DevTools → Application tab: Cookies, Local Storage, Session Storage.
Inspect key, value, TTL (for cookies), domain and path.
Redux / Zustand: Redux DevTools or console.log the state.
TYPICAL MISTAKE

A test clears cookies but not localStorage. A JWT or state from a previous test remains in localStorage and "leaks" into the next test — authentication passes without a real login.

Layer 2 — HTTP Browser Cache

The browser caches HTTP responses to disk according to Cache-Control and Expires directives, and validates freshness via conditional requests with ETag or Last-Modified. A 304 Not Modified response means "data hasn't changed — use the cache".

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 2
DevTools → Network → Status column: 200 vs 304 (from cache).
Size column: "(memory cache)" or "(disk cache)" indicates a cache hit.
Response headers: Cache-Control, ETag, Age.
TYPICAL MISTAKE

A test receives 304 and treats it as a successful "200 OK". In reality it is verifying a stale cached response. For testing, always disable cache (DevTools → Network → Disable cache) or add Cache-Control: no-cache to the request.

Layer 3 — CDN / Proxy Cache

A CDN (Cloudflare, Fastly, AWS CloudFront) places cached responses on edge servers close to the user. A reverse proxy (Nginx, Varnish) can cache backend responses. Key response header: X-Cache: HIT or X-Cache: MISS.

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 3
Inspect response headers:
X-Cache: HIT / X-Cache: MISS
CF-Cache-Status: HIT (Cloudflare)
Age — how many seconds the response has been in cache.
Tool: curl -I https://example.com/api/data
TYPICAL MISTAKE

Data is updated in the database but the CDN keeps serving the old cache for another hour. Clearing the application cache does not clear the CDN. A separate CDN Cache Purge API call is needed, or you must wait for TTL to expire.

Layer 4 — API Gateway Cache

Some API Gateways (AWS API Gateway, Kong, Apigee) support response caching at the gateway level. If caching is enabled, a repeated request to the same endpoint with the same parameters may never reach the microservice.

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 4
Check API Gateway configuration: is there a cache policy for this endpoint?
Response headers: some gateways add X-Cache or their own headers.
Compare response times: a cache hit is significantly faster than a cache miss.
TYPICAL MISTAKE

A GET request with ?page=1 is cached. A POST request that mutates data completes successfully, but the next GET still returns the gateway's stale cache — the gateway has no knowledge that the data changed.

Layer 5 — App In-memory Cache

Data is cached directly in the process memory of the application: a Map, an LRU cache (Caffeine for Java, node-lru-cache for Node.js). Fastest option, but data is not shared across instances and is lost on service restart.

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 5
Check application logs or metrics: cache hit rate, cache size.
In a test: update data via API → GET → if response is stale, in-memory cache was not invalidated.
Restarting the service clears the in-memory cache — the first request after restart is always a cache miss.
TYPICAL MISTAKE

With horizontal scaling each instance holds its own in-memory cache. A write to one instance does not invalidate the cache in others. Different requests from the same user may hit different instances and receive different responses.

Layer 6 — Redis / Distributed Cache

An external distributed cache — a separate process (Redis, Memcached) accessible to all application instances. Data survives service restarts when Redis persistence is enabled. The standard for horizontally scaled systems.

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 6
redis-cli: GET key — check existence and value.
TTL key — seconds remaining until expiry.
MONITOR — watch all commands in real time (for debugging).
After a DB update: verify the Redis key was deleted or updated.
TYPICAL MISTAKE

Data is updated in the DB but cache invalidation did not happen (logic bug or race condition). Redis keeps serving the stale version until TTL expires. A test that writes and immediately reads may not catch this — also test after a separate update request.

Layer 7 — Database

The database engine has its own internal cache: InnoDB buffer pool (MySQL/MariaDB), shared_buffers (PostgreSQL). Repeated SELECT queries on the same data execute much faster thanks to cached pages in memory.

HOW TO CHECK — LAYER 7
EXPLAIN ANALYZE (PostgreSQL) or EXPLAIN (MySQL) — inspect query plan and actual execution time.
Slow query log — log queries that exceed a time threshold.
First query after a DB restart — always slower (cold cache).
TYPICAL MISTAKE

Performance is measured only on a "warm" cache — the DB has already been primed by earlier queries. After a deploy or restart the first requests are significantly slower. Performance tests that run repeatedly without resetting state will show unrealistically optimistic results.

Cache investigation order

STRATEGY

Start at the top layers — browser and CDN. Most visible cache problems live there. Move down only after the upper layers have been ruled out.

① Open DevTools Network → Disable cache → reload
② Inspect response headers: X-Cache, CF-Cache-Status, Age
③ Try a different browser or incognito mode
④ Make the request via curl — bypassing the browser cache
⑤ Check Redis: redis-cli GET <key>
⑥ Query the DB directly: is the data actually fresh there?

02 Load balancer and cache COMPONENT
↑ top
A common misconception: a load balancer is not a cache. It does not store or return responses. A load balancer only forwards the request to one of the available servers. Caching is the responsibility of a CDN, reverse proxy, API Gateway, or the application itself.
ComponentCaches responses?Notes
CDN (Cloudflare, CloudFront)YesStores HTTP responses on globally distributed edge servers
Reverse Proxy (Nginx, Varnish)YesCan cache backend responses (requires explicit configuration)
API Gateway (Kong, AWS APIGW)PartiallyOptional caching, must be enabled per endpoint
Load Balancer (HAProxy, AWS ALB)NoOnly routes TCP/HTTP connections, does not store responses
MicroserviceYesIn-memory cache or Redis — the service's own responsibility

If a stale cached response is being returned, look in the CDN, reverse proxy, or API Gateway — not in the load balancer. The load balancer is transparent to data — it neither reads nor stores response bodies.

03 Browser Storage CONCEPT
↑ top
The browser provides three client-side storage mechanisms: localStorage, sessionStorage, and IndexedDB. Each has its own purpose and constraints. A QA engineer needs to understand the differences to correctly clear state between tests and properly verify persisted state.

localStorage

Persistent key-value storage. Data survives across sessions (closing and reopening the browser). Scoped to the origin. Synchronous API — blocks the main thread for large amounts of data. Typical limit is ~5–10 MB depending on the browser.

sessionStorage

Identical API to localStorage, but data exists only for the current tab. Closing the tab deletes the data. A new tab gets its own isolated storage, even for the same origin. Useful for multi-step wizard forms and temporary in-flight state.

IndexedDB

A full NoSQL database in the browser with an asynchronous API. Supports storing structured objects (not just strings), transactions, indexes, and large data volumes. Used in PWAs for offline mode and in apps with complex local state.

Comparison

localStoragesessionStorageIndexedDB
Capacity~5–10 MB~5 MBHundreds of MB+
LifetimePersistentCurrent tab onlyPersistent
ScopeOriginTabOrigin
APISynchronousSynchronousAsynchronous
Data typeStringsStringsAny JS objects
TransactionsNoNoYes
QA TEST ANGLES — BROWSER STORAGE
① Verify that on logout all user data is removed from localStorage and sessionStorage.
② Verify overflow behavior: write more than the limit → expect QuotaExceededError.
③ Verify tab isolation: sessionStorage data from one tab is not accessible in another.
④ Verify that sensitive data (passwords, tokens) is not stored in plain text.
⑤ IndexedDB in a PWA: verify offline mode — data is accessible without a network connection after the first load.

Documentation: MDN — Web Storage API · MDN — IndexedDB API

04 Cache invalidation triggers CONCEPT
↑ top

Invalidation triggers by layer

Browser

TriggerHow it works
TTL expiredCache-Control: max-age=3600 — after 3600 seconds browser makes a fresh request
ETag mismatchBrowser sends If-None-Match: "abc123" — server compares, returns 200 with new content if changed
Last-Modified changedBrowser sends If-Modified-Since — server checks file modification date
Hard reloadCtrl+Shift+R — browser bypasses cache entirely
Cache-Control: no-storeServer prohibits caching altogether

CDN

TriggerHow it works
TTL expiredEdge node holds a copy for N seconds, then fetches fresh from origin
Explicit API purgeDeveloper calls CDN API: "invalidate this URL" — used after deploys
URL versioningstyle.css?v=2 — new URL, CDN treats it as a new resource with no cache
Cache-Control: no-cache from originCDN does not cache the response
Purge allFull cache flush — typically after a major release

Reverse proxy

TriggerHow it works
TTL expiredproxy_cache_valid 200 10m — entry deleted after 10 minutes
Cache-Control: no-store from backendNginx does not cache this response
Cache key changeDifferent query params or headers = different cache entry
Manual purgeDelete cache files on disk or use proxy_cache_purge module

Application cache (Redis)

TriggerHow it works
TTL expiredSET key value EX 300 — Redis deletes the entry automatically after 300 seconds
Explicit delete after writeAfter UPDATE in DB — code calls DEL cache:user:123
Event-driven invalidationService publishes UserUpdated event → subscriber deletes the relevant cache key
Pattern-based purgeDEL cache:orders:* — delete all keys matching a prefix

Database

TriggerHow it works
Write operationINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — database invalidates internal query cache for affected tables
Replication lagReplica receives changes from primary with a delay — returns stale data until synced

Invalidation after unsafe HTTP methods

HTTP methods are divided into safe and unsafe.

Safe — do not modify state on the server: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Can be cached.
Unsafe — modify state: POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE. Must not be cached, and their successful execution must invalidate related cache entries.

Per HTTP specification (RFC 9110) — after a successful POST, PUT, PATCH, or DELETE, the browser must invalidate cached responses for the same URI.

GET  /api/orders/123     → response cached in browser
PUT  /api/orders/123     → successful update
GET  /api/orders/123     → browser does NOT return cached version,
                           makes a fresh request

Browser handles this automatically for the same URI if the response was 200, 201, or 204.

CDN and reverse proxy do not know your data changed — they have no business logic awareness. Invalidation here is always explicit: purge API call after a successful write, URL versioning, or short TTL on frequently changing resources.

Application cache (Redis) — the most common pattern is invalidate-on-write:

PUT /api/orders/123
  → update in database
  → DEL cache:orders:123   ← explicit deletion
  → return 200

If this step is skipped, the next GET returns stale data from cache.

Method-specific invalidation strategy

The correct invalidation scope depends on which method was used:

MethodWhat changedWhat to invalidate
PUT /orders/123Known specific resourcecache:orders:123
PATCH /orders/123Known specific resourcecache:orders:123
DELETE /orders/123Resource removedcache:orders:123 + any list containing it
POST /ordersNew resource created, ID unknownCollection: cache:orders:list:*

PUT and PATCH are idempotent — repeating the call with the same data produces the same result. This makes the invalidation target predictable: you always know exactly which key to delete.

POST is not idempotent — a repeat call may create a duplicate. The invalidation target is less precise: you must invalidate the collection, not just a specific entry.

Cache stampede

When TTL for a large number of entries expires simultaneously, all requests go to the origin at once — a sudden spike in load. Solved with jitter: adding a random offset to TTL values so entries expire at different times rather than all together.

base TTL: 300 seconds
with jitter: 300 + random(0, 60) seconds per entry
QA TESTING ANGLES — CACHE INVALIDATION
Cache freshness after write. After PUT or PATCH on a resource → the next GET on the same URI returns updated data, not the cached previous version.

Delete invalidation. After DELETE on a resource → the next GET returns 404, not the old cached response.

Collection invalidation after POST. After POST creating a new resource → GET on the collection endpoint includes the new item.

No caching on sensitive endpoints. Verify Cache-Control: no-store is set on endpoints returning personal, financial, or session data — they must never be cached at any layer.

TTL boundary. Test behaviour immediately after TTL expiry — the first request after expiry should return fresh data, not a stale hit.

Replication lag (flaky test root cause). A test writes data then immediately reads it — and does not find it, because the read went to a replica that has not yet synced. First hypothesis for any data inconsistency in test environments: cache or replication lag, not a bug.

Parallel writes. Two concurrent PUT requests on the same resource → the final state is consistent, cache does not contain an intermediate state from the losing write.

Response headers on mutating endpoints. POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE responses must not contain Cache-Control: max-age — mutating endpoints should never be cached.
KEY TAKEAWAYS

Cache lives at every layer — browser, CDN, proxy, application, database. Each has its own invalidation rules.
Invalidation is either time-based (TTL expires) or event-based (explicit delete after a write).
Unsafe HTTP methods must trigger invalidation — browser does this automatically, every other layer requires explicit handling.
POST invalidates collections. PUT, PATCH, DELETE invalidate specific resources.
Replication lag and stale cache are the two most common causes of unexpected data behaviour in test environments. Always check these before assuming a bug.

05 HTTP Caching — QA Checklist by Method and Layer CHECKLIST
↑ top

Quick reference matrix

MethodBrowserCDNReverse ProxyAPI GatewayApp Cache (Redis)Database
GET✓ Cache✓ Cache✓ CacheConditionalConditionalInternal
HEAD✓ Cache✓ Cache✓ CacheConditionalNoNo
OPTIONSPreflight TTL onlyNoNoNoNoNo
POSTNoNoNoNoInvalidatesInvalidates
PUTNoNoNoNoInvalidatesInvalidates
PATCHNoNoNoNoInvalidatesInvalidates
DELETENoNoNoNoInvalidatesInvalidates

GET

The only method that should be cached at every layer. All caching infrastructure is designed around GET responses.

BROWSER CACHE
SHOULD see
— Cache-Control: max-age=N on public static resources (CSS, JS, images)
— Cache-Control: private, max-age=N on authenticated or personalised responses
— ETag: "abc123" or Last-Modified: <date> on any resource that requires revalidation
— On a repeat request — browser sends If-None-Match: "abc123" or If-Modified-Since: <date>
— Server returns 304 Not Modified with an empty body if content has not changed
— Vary: Accept-Encoding if the response is compressed

SHOULD NOT see
— Cache-Control: no-store on public static resources — this actively prohibits caching
— Cache-Control: max-age=N on responses containing personal, financial, or session data
— Missing ETag or Last-Modified on large resources — a missed optimisation, every request downloads the full content
— Pragma: no-cache — a deprecated HTTP/1.0 directive, replace with Cache-Control
— Expires header without Cache-Control — legacy, unreliable

How to check
— DevTools → Network tab → inspect response headers on the first request
— Repeat the request — status should be 304, not 200, if content has not changed
— Hard reload (Ctrl+Shift+R) — forced request, status must be 200
— Check the Size column in DevTools — cached responses show (disk cache) or (memory cache)
CDN (CloudFront, Cloudflare)
SHOULD see
— X-Cache: Hit (CloudFront) or CF-Cache-Status: HIT (Cloudflare) on repeat requests
— Age: N — seconds the response has been in the CDN cache
— Cache-Control: public, s-maxage=N for CDN-specific TTL separate from the browser TTL
— Vary: Accept-Encoding if the CDN compresses responses
— ETag forwarded from origin so downstream can perform revalidation

SHOULD NOT see
— CDN caching responses with Cache-Control: private — private responses must not be stored in a shared cache
— CDN caching responses that contain Set-Cookie — unless explicitly and intentionally configured
— X-Cache: Hit on authenticated API responses without Vary: Authorization — different users will receive each other's responses
— Age value exceeding the configured max-age — indicates a misconfigured TTL

How to check
— Send the same GET twice — the first should be MISS, the second HIT
— Verify that the Age header increments on repeated requests
— Send a request with a different Authorization header — should be a MISS, not served from a previous user's cache
— Purge the URL via CDN API, then request it — should be a MISS
REVERSE PROXY (Nginx)
SHOULD see
— X-Cache-Status: HIT (Nginx with proxy_cache) on cached responses
— Cache-Control headers from upstream forwarded or overridden according to configuration
— Age header if Nginx adds it

SHOULD NOT see
— Nginx caching responses with Cache-Control: no-store from upstream
— Nginx caching responses with Set-Cookie — standard Nginx behaviour ignores them, but verify your configuration
— Cached response served after upstream data changes before TTL expires — expected behaviour, but important to know the staleness window

How to check
— Check Nginx access logs — cache HIT vs MISS
— Compare response time: HIT is significantly faster than MISS
— Set a short proxy_cache_valid TTL in the test environment, confirm that a stale response is served until expiry
API GATEWAY (Kong, AWS API Gateway)
SHOULD see
— Caching enabled only for explicitly configured routes — not globally by default
— Cache-Control headers respected — the gateway must not cache what upstream marked as no-store
— Reduced response time on repeated identical requests when caching is enabled
— Cache key includes all relevant parameters — URI, query string, and if personalised — the Authorization header

SHOULD NOT see
— Gateway caching authenticated endpoint responses without scoping the cache key per user — a critical security misconfiguration
— Gateway caching error responses (4xx, 5xx) — only 200 should be cache-eligible
— Cached responses served after upstream data changes within TTL without explicit invalidation

How to check
— Send the same GET twice with caching enabled — the second should be faster
— Change a query parameter — should be a cache miss, not the previous response
— Two users with different tokens request the same URI — each should receive their own data
APP CACHE (Redis / Memcached)
SHOULD see
— Cache key follows a consistent naming convention: resource:id, e.g. orders:123
— TTL set on every key — no keys without TTL on frequently changing data
— Cache miss falls through to the DB and stores the result for next time
— Measurable difference in response time between cache hit and cache miss

SHOULD NOT see
— Cached results for queries that must always be fresh (e.g. account balance, stock count)
— Keys without TTL on mutable data — permanently stale data if there is a bug in the invalidation logic
— Cache storing large objects in full when only a subset of fields is needed — wastes memory

How to check
— redis-cli GET orders:123 — verify the key exists after the first GET request
— Check TTL: redis-cli TTL orders:123 — should return remaining seconds, not -1 (no TTL)
— Delete the key manually, repeat GET — response time increases (DB fallthrough)
— Update the resource, verify the Redis key is deleted or updated
DATABASE
SHOULD see
— Internal query plan cache used for repeated identical queries — the same query executes faster on the second run
— Buffer pool (PostgreSQL shared_buffers, MySQL innodb_buffer_pool) keeps frequently accessed data in memory

SHOULD NOT see
— Stale query results after PUT or DELETE — the internal cache must be invalidated automatically on write

How to check
— Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE in PostgreSQL before and after a repeat execution — the second run shows lower cost
— In test environments: confirm that a fresh SELECT after UPDATE returns the updated values immediately

HEAD

Identical caching rules to GET — same headers, TTL, revalidation mechanism. The only difference is that the response body is empty.

ALL LAYERS
Apply the same checklist as for GET at every layer.

Additional check: ETag and Last-Modified must be present in the HEAD response — the client uses HEAD specifically to check whether content has changed before downloading via GET. If these headers are absent from HEAD, the optimisation is pointless.

OPTIONS

Used primarily for CORS preflight. Not cached by standard caching infrastructure — only the browser caches the preflight result.

BROWSER CACHE
SHOULD see
— Access-Control-Max-Age: N — how long the browser caches the preflight result in seconds
— Subsequent requests to the same endpoint within this window do not trigger a new preflight

SHOULD NOT see
— Access-Control-Max-Age: 0 or absent — browser sends a preflight on every request, significant overhead

How to check
— DevTools → Network — the OPTIONS request appears once, then disappears for subsequent calls within the TTL
— Temporarily set Access-Control-Max-Age: 0 — the OPTIONS request reappears on every call
CDN · REVERSE PROXY · API GATEWAY · APP CACHE · DATABASE
OPTIONS is not cached at these layers. Nothing to check.

POST

Must not be cached at any layer. The response MUST NOT be stored. Execution must trigger invalidation of the related GET cache.

BROWSER
SHOULD see
— Cache-Control: no-store in the response
— No ETag or Last-Modified in the response

SHOULD NOT see
— Cache-Control: max-age=N in the response
— Browser reusing a previous POST response on retry

How to check
— DevTools — POST responses must never show (disk cache) or (memory cache)
— Repeat the POST — it must always reach the server, with no cache interference
CDN · REVERSE PROXY
SHOULD NOT see
— CDN or proxy returning a cached response to a POST request — this means a previous POST response was incorrectly stored
— X-Cache: HIT on any POST response

How to check
— Send the same POST twice — both must reach the origin server (verify origin logs)
— The X-Cache header should be absent or show MISS / BYPASS
API GATEWAY
SHOULD see
— POST requests always forwarded to upstream — never served from cache
— Caching plugin/policy explicitly disabled for POST routes

SHOULD NOT see
— Any caching directives applied to POST endpoints
APP CACHE (Redis) — invalidation
SHOULD see
— After a successful POST creating a new resource — collection cache keys are deleted
— Example: POST /orders succeeds → DEL cache:orders:list:*
— New resource is available on the next GET of the collection

SHOULD NOT see
— GET of the collection returning a stale list after POST — new item absent

How to check
— POST /orders → immediately GET /orders → new item must be present
— Check Redis: the collection key must be absent after POST (deleted), not containing stale data
DATABASE
SHOULD see
— INSERT invalidates the internal query cache for the affected table — the next SELECT returns fresh results

How to check
— SELECT count before and after INSERT — count must reflect the new row immediately

PUT

Must not be cached. Response must not be stored. Must invalidate the cache for the specific resource.

BROWSER · CDN · REVERSE PROXY · API GATEWAY
SHOULD see
— Cache-Control: no-store in the response
— No Age header
— No X-Cache: HIT

SHOULD NOT see
— Any layer returning a cached PUT response
— Cache-Control: max-age in the response

How to check
— PUT, then immediately GET the same URI — GET must return the updated resource, not a cached old version
— Check origin server logs — both the PUT and the subsequent GET must appear (GET not served from cache)
APP CACHE (Redis) — invalidation
SHOULD see
— Specific resource key deleted after PUT: DEL cache:orders:123
— Next GET falls through to the DB and repopulates the cache

SHOULD NOT see
— GET /orders/123 returning old values after a successful PUT
— Redis key containing data that predates the PUT

How to check
— PUT /orders/123 with a changed field → GET /orders/123 → changed field must be present
— redis-cli GET orders:123 after PUT — key must be absent (deleted) or contain the updated data

PATCH

Same rules as PUT. Must not be cached. Must invalidate the specific resource.

ALL LAYERS
Apply the full PUT checklist above.

Important note: PATCH modifies a subset of fields — ensure that cache invalidation covers the full resource, not just the modified fields. A partial cache update is more dangerous than a full delete and reload.

DELETE

Must not be cached at any layer. Must invalidate both the specific resource and any collection that contained it.

BROWSER · CDN · REVERSE PROXY · API GATEWAY
SHOULD see
— Cache-Control: no-store in the DELETE response
— After DELETE — the next GET of the same URI returns 404 from the server, not a cached 200

SHOULD NOT see
— Cache-Control: max-age in the DELETE response
— X-Cache: HIT in the DELETE response — means a previous DELETE response was cached, subsequent DELETEs never reached the server
— GET of the deleted resource returning 200 from cache

How to check
— DELETE /orders/123 → GET /orders/123 → must be 404, not 200
— Hard reload or disable cache → repeat GET → if the result changed, the previous 200 was from cache
— Send DELETE twice — the second call must return 404 from the server, not a cached 200 from the first
APP CACHE (Redis) — invalidation
SHOULD see
— Specific resource key deleted: DEL cache:orders:123
— All collection keys that contained this resource deleted: DEL cache:orders:list:*
— Dependent resource keys deleted if applicable (e.g. the user's order list)

SHOULD NOT see
— GET /orders/123 returning data after DELETE — resource still in Redis
— Collection GET /orders still containing the deleted item

How to check
— DELETE /orders/123 → redis-cli GET orders:123 → must return nil
— DELETE /orders/123 → GET /orders → deleted item must not appear in the list
DATABASE
SHOULD see
— DELETE invalidates the internal cache for the affected rows — a SELECT immediately after returns an empty result for that row

How to check
— SELECT by ID before deletion — row exists. DELETE. SELECT again — row absent. No stale result.

Summary by layer — what to always check

ANY MUTATING METHOD (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE)
— Response must contain Cache-Control: no-store
— No ETag, Last-Modified, Age, or X-Cache: HIT in the response
— The next GET on the same URI must reach the origin server, not any cache layer
— Verify that Redis keys are deleted after the operation completes
— Verify that collection endpoints reflect the change — not just the specific resource endpoint
GET
— Public static resources must have max-age and ETag
— Authenticated or personalised responses must have private or no-store
— A repeat request returns 304 or is served from cache with X-Cache: HIT
— The Age header must be present and incrementing on CDN-cached responses
RED FLAGS AT ANY LAYER

— Cache-Control: max-age in a DELETE, PUT, PATCH, or POST response
— X-Cache: HIT in any mutating method response
— GET returning 200 with stale data immediately after a successful write
— Redis key with TTL -1 (no TTL) on mutable data
— Access-Control-Max-Age absent or zero in OPTIONS responses
